concept.title: Moonshot: The Mathematics of Dyson's Intelligence Explosion
concept.concept_description: Formalize Freeman Dyson's idea that intelligence grows without limit in the deep future. Define: 'intelligence growth rate' as the rate at which a civilization discovers new theorems. Prove: if the growth rate is superexponential (faster than 2^(2^n)), then the civilization discovers ALL theorems of ZFC in finite time (by compactness). Show: if the growth rate is merely exponential (2^n), then there exist theorems that are NEVER discovered (Gödel). Conjecture: the growth rate is bounded by the physical computation limit (Bekenstein bound) at ~10^120 ops in the observable universe. Explore: does the intelligence explosion require new mathematics (theorems not expressible in current systems)?

concept.title: White's Quadratic Exchange Conjecture (Part 3)
concept.concept_description: While White's conjecture on symmetric exchanges (Part 2) is false, the weaker Part 3 remains open: for any matroid M and any two multisets of bases B and B' with the same multiset union of elements, it is possible to obtain B' from B by repeatedly replacing two bases with any two other bases having the same multiset union. This is equivalent to the toric ideal of the matroid basis exchange ring being generated by quadratic binomials.
concept.mathematical_framing: While White's conjecture on symmetric exchanges (Part 2) is false, the weaker Part 3 remains open: for any matroid M and any two multisets of bases B and B' with the same multiset union of elements, it is possible to obtain B' from B by repeatedly replacing two bases with any two other bases having the same multiset union. This is equivalent to the toric ideal of the matroid basis exchange ring being generated by quadratic binomials.
concept.lean_guess: The conjecture could be approached by demonstrating that the toric ideal of any matroid basis exchange ring is generated by quadratic binomials. One could use tropical geometry or Gröbner basis techniques, or attempt an inductive proof on matroid minors, extending the methods used for specific matroid classes like uniform or graphic matroids.

concept.title: Categorifying the quantum binomial product rule via filtrations of plethystic modules
concept.concept_description: We conjecture that for any field F and integers n ≥ m ≥ 0, d ≥ 0, the field‑independent filtration of Δ^(n,m)Sym^dE described in the paper yields graded pieces whose characters are exactly the quantum binomial coefficients appearing in the product rule (Rel2) for Lusztig’s quantum Cartan elements. In particular, the i‑th quotient is isomorphic to Δ^(n‑i,m‑i)Sym^(d‑i)E and its formal character equals s_(n‑i,m‑i) ∘ s_(d‑i).
concept.mathematical_framing: We conjecture that for any field F and integers n ≥ m ≥ 0, d ≥ 0, the field‑independent filtration of Δ^(n,m)Sym^dE described in the paper yields graded pieces whose characters are exactly the quantum binomial coefficients appearing in the product rule (Rel2) for Lusztig’s quantum Cartan elements. In particular, the i‑th quotient is isomorphic to Δ^(n‑i,m‑i)Sym^(d‑i)E and its formal character equals s_(n‑i,m‑i) ∘ s_(d‑i).
concept.lean_guess: Use the symmetric functions model for Weyl modules (as in the paper) to prove by induction on d that the filtration is functorial and that successive quotients have characters given by the plethystic product s_(n‑i,m‑i) ∘ s_(d‑i). The key step is to establish a bijection between the standard basis of the graded pieces and the combinatorial descriptions of the quantum binomial coefficients, mirroring the proof of the product rule (Rel2).

concept.title: Explicit Threshold for No-(k+1)-in-line: f_k(n) = kn for all k ≥ 3 and n ≥ k
concept.concept_description: The paper proves that for k ≥ 3 and sufficiently large n, the maximum number of points in an n × n grid with no k+1 collinear points equals kn. This conjecture asserts that 'sufficiently large' can be replaced by the explicit threshold n ≥ k. Note that for n ≤ k the whole grid has no k+1 collinear points so f_k(n) = n², and for n = k we get f_k(k) = k² = k·k, making n ≥ k the natural boundary. The conjecture predicts that for all k ≥ 3 and n ≥ k, the trivial upper bound kn is always achievable.
concept.mathematical_framing: The paper proves that for k ≥ 3 and sufficiently large n, the maximum number of points in an n × n grid with no k+1 collinear points equals kn. This conjecture asserts that 'sufficiently large' can be replaced by the explicit threshold n ≥ k. Note that for n ≤ k the whole grid has no k+1 collinear points so f_k(n) = n², and for n = k we get f_k(k) = k² = k·k, making n ≥ k the natural boundary. The conjecture predicts that for all k ≥ 3 and n ≥ k, the trivial upper bound kn is always achievable.
concept.lean_guess: The paper's approach splits into: (1) handling 'heavy' lines via pseudorandom hypergraph matchings (Ehard-Glock-Joos), (2) crude deletion for remaining violations, (3) randomized switching to recover near-optimal size. To push 'sufficiently large n' down to n ≥ k, one would need to make each step effective with explicit bounds. The hypergraph matching step likely requires the most careful analysis for small n. A computer-verified case analysis for small n (up to some explicit bound) combined with the asymptotic argument for larger n could work. The key is determining whether the o(n) deletion/swinging losses can be controlled when n is close to k.

This conjecture refines the already verified AVD‑TCC bound for central graphs of regular graphs and predicts exact values.
concept.mathematical_framing: For every regular graph $G$ of degree $d\ge 2$ (i.e., $\Delta(G)=d$ and $G$ is $d$‑regular), we conjecture that the central graph $C(G)$ achieves the maximal possible AVD‑total chromatic number, namely $\chi''_{a}(C(G)) = d+3$, except in the degenerate case where $G$ is a complete graph $K_{d+1}$ (for which $\chi''_{a}(C(G)) = d+2$). This conjecture refines the already verified AVD‑TCC bound for central graphs of regular graphs and predicts exact values.
concept.lean_guess: The conjecture is approached in two parts. 1. **Lower bound**: Show that any AVD‑total coloring of $C(G)$ must use at least $d+3$ colors by constructing a small subgraph (e.g., a copy of $K_{d+1}$ or a suitable $d$‑regular subgraph) whose AVD‑total chromatic number is known to be $d+3$ (using results of Zhang et al. or the AVD‑TCC). This yields $\chi''_{a}(C(G)) \ge d+3$. 2. **Upper bound**: Build an explicit AVD‑total coloring of $C(G)$ with $d+3$ colors. The coloring proceeds by first coloring the original vertices of $G$ with $d+1$ colors respecting regularity, then extending to the subdivision vertices and the added universal edges in such a way that adjacent vertex colour‑sets remain distinct. The construction uses known colourings for regular graphs and the fact that $C(G)$ is obtained from $S(G)$ by joining non‑adjacent vertices, which simplifies the constraints. Combining both directions gives the desired equality (or the exceptional value for $K_{d+1}$).

concept.title: Product Hilton-Milner theorem for large n
concept.concept_description: For integers n, k, ℓ with n > 100·ℓ·k² and 3 ≤ ℓ < k, if F ⊆ ([n] choose k) and G ⊆ ([n] choose ℓ) are non-trivial cross-intersecting families (i.e., ⋂_{F∈F} F = ∅ and ⋂_{G∈G} G = ∅, and F ∩ G ≠ ∅ for all F ∈ F, G ∈ G), then |F|·|G| ≤ h(n,k)·(n-1 choose ℓ-1), where h(n,k) = (n-1 choose k-1) - (n-k-1 choose k-1) + 1 is the Hilton-Milner bound.
concept.mathematical_framing: For integers n, k, ℓ with n > 100·ℓ·k² and 3 ≤ ℓ < k, if F ⊆ ([n] choose k) and G ⊆ ([n] choose ℓ) are non-trivial cross-intersecting families (i.e., ⋂_{F∈F} F = ∅ and ⋂_{G∈G} G = ∅, and F ∩ G ≠ ∅ for all F ∈ F, G ∈ G), then |F|·|G| ≤ h(n,k)·(n-1 choose ℓ-1), where h(n,k) = (n-1 choose k-1) - (n-k-1 choose k-1) + 1 is the Hilton-Milner bound.
concept.lean_guess: First formalize the classical Hilton-Milner theorem as a lemma. Then formalize the notion of cross-intersecting families and non-triviality. The key structural insight from the paper is analyzing 2-cover graphs of cross-intersecting families and bounding the size of families with small minimal covers. The proof proceeds by case analysis on the structure of minimal covers of F and G, showing that non-HM-type configurations yield strictly smaller products when n > 100ℓk².
